Under the "Pets" section on pages 1–2 of your Room Rental Agreement:
> "No pets of any kind may be kept in the house or yard, even for a short visit. The only exception is fish in one tank of 10 gallons or less, kept in the Tenant's room."

Because a cat is a pet and not fish in a tank of 10 gallons or less, keeping one violates the lease. Under Fla. Stat. § 83.56(2)(b), keeping an unauthorized pet is a lease violation for which the landlord may give you a written 7-day notice to cure (remove the pet). If the pet is not removed within 7 days, or if the violation recurs within 12 months after notice, the landlord can terminate your rental agreement.

*(Note: If the cat is a service animal or an emotional support animal for a disability under federal or Florida fair housing laws, those laws operate outside standard lease pet restrictions; however, the lease itself strictly prohibits pets.)*

# Deposit not returned

Rests on 83.49 (the deposit) and 83.505 (notices by e-mail). Read a section in full with get_statute_section.

## First, whether this applies

- 83.49 does not cover every deposit: "This section does not apply to transient rentals by hotels or motels as defined in chapter 509 or in those instances in which the amount of rent or deposit, or both, is regulated by law or by rules or regulations of a public body" (83.49(4)).
- College housing may be outside part II. It does not apply to "Residency or detention in a facility, whether public or private, when residence or detention is incidental to the provision of medical, geriatric, educational, counseling, religious, or similar services." (83.42(1)). Read 83.42 before telling the tenant either way, and say what you would need to know.
- Money the lease calls nonrefundable may fall under 83.491. Read it before treating that money as outside 83.49.

## Facts the answer turns on

Read the lease first. Ask the tenant only plain facts, one or two at a time. Note each fact with note_fact under these names, dates written YYYY-MM-DD; a date counts only once the tenant has confirmed it.

- lease_end_date: the date the rental agreement ended. move_out_date: the date they moved out and returned the keys.
- Whether they moved out before the lease's end, or had a month-to-month or other periodic tenancy.
- If so: what written notice they gave before leaving, how it reached the landlord, and whether it gave an address.
- What the landlord sent about keeping any of the deposit: what it said, how it came, the date on it (claim_notice_date), and the date the tenant received it (claim_received_date).
- Whether they and the landlord signed an addendum agreeing to notices by e-mail.

## Option 1: the whole deposit, because no notice of a claim came in time

All three conditions must be met. Settle each one from the facts: met, not met, the tenant can tell us, or not settled.

1. **No proper notice of a claim reached the tenant.** The rule: "If the landlord intends to impose a claim on the deposit, the landlord must, within 30 days after the termination of the rental agreement, provide the tenant written notice by certified mail to the tenant’s last known mailing address or by e-mail in accordance with s. 83.505 of his or her intention to impose a claim on the deposit and the reason for imposing the claim." (83.49(3)(a)). E-mail counts only "if the parties have signed an addendum to the rental agreement that the parties specifically agree to the electronic delivery of notices" (83.505(1)).
   - Nothing in writing about keeping any of it arrived: met.
   - A notice came by certified mail, or by e-mail under a signed addendum: not met. Go to option 2.
   - A notice came some other way (regular mail, a text, a portal message, by hand): not settled. Give both readings and choose neither. One: it is not the required notice, so the claim is forfeited (the forfeiture sentence below). The other: a notice the tenant actually received in time is enough, since 83.505 "does not preclude service of notices by any other means permitted by law." (83.505(6)). Under that reading, go on to option 2 as well, and say what each reading means for the tenant's money.
2. **The 30 days have passed.** Call count_days(lease_end_date, 30). If it has not passed, a notice may still come in time, so this option is not open yet.
   - If the tenant moved out before the lease's end date, which date ends the rental agreement is not settled. Call both count_days(lease_end_date, 30) and count_days(move_out_date, 30), and give both readings. The lease end date: 83.49(3)(a) begins "Upon the vacating of the premises for termination of the rental agreement" (83.49(3)(a)), naming vacating and termination as two things. The move-out date: the required disclosure tells tenants the notice comes "WITHIN 30 DAYS AFTER YOU MOVE OUT" (83.49(2)(d)).
3. **The landlord was not relieved of the notice.** A tenant who left early, or had a periodic tenancy, must give notice first. Who: "Except when otherwise provided by the terms of a written rental agreement, any tenant who vacates or abandons the premises before the expiration of the term specified in the rental agreement, or any tenant who vacates or abandons premises which are the subject of a tenancy from week to week, month to month, quarter to quarter, or year to year," (83.49(5)). How: "must give at least 7 days’ written notice by certified mail or personal delivery to the landlord before vacating or abandoning the premises, which notice must include the address where the tenant may be reached." (83.49(5)).
   - The tenant stayed to the lease's end and had no periodic tenancy: met.
   - They gave that notice, with an address, on or before the date count_days(move_out_date, -7) gives: met.
   - The lease sets a different rule on notice before leaving, and they followed it: met. Read the lease's clause.
   - Otherwise not met: "Failure to give such notice relieves the landlord of the notice requirement of paragraph (3)(a) but does not waive any right the tenant may have to the security deposit or any part of it." (83.49(5)). Say both halves: the landlord's silence forfeits nothing, and the tenant keeps the right to the deposit.

If all three are met: "If the landlord fails to give the required written notice within the 30-day period, he or she forfeits the right to impose a claim upon the security deposit and may not seek a setoff against the deposit but may file an action for damages after returning the security deposit to the tenant." (83.49(3)(a)). Say both halves: the whole deposit comes back, and the landlord may still sue for damages after.

## Option 2: the balance after a notice of a claim

When a notice of a claim came (or under the reading that one that came another way counts): "Unless the tenant objects to the imposition of the landlord’s claim or the amount thereof within 15 days after receipt of the landlord’s notice of intention to impose a claim, the landlord may then deduct the amount of his or her claim and shall remit the balance of the deposit to the tenant within 30 days after the date of the notice of intention to impose a claim for damages." (83.49(3)(b)).

- The tenant's last day to object in writing: count_days(claim_received_date, 15).
- The landlord's last day to send the balance: count_days(claim_notice_date, 30).
- Not objecting is not the end: "The failure of the tenant to make a timely objection does not waive any rights of the tenant to seek damages in a separate action." (83.49(3)(b)).

## The 15-day return

When the landlord intends no claim: "if the landlord does not intend to impose a claim on the security deposit, the landlord must return the security deposit, together with interest if otherwise required, within 15 days after the termination of the rental agreement" (83.49(3)(a)). The date: count_days(lease_end_date, 15). Passing it forfeits nothing while the 30 days for a notice of a claim are still running.

## Court costs and fees

Only if someone sues, and only for the winner: "If either party institutes an action in a court of competent jurisdiction to adjudicate the party’s right to the security deposit, the prevailing party is entitled to receive his or her court costs plus a reasonable fee for his or her attorney." (83.49(3)(c)).

## Mistakes to avoid

- Writing any date that count_days did not give you, or comparing dates yourself.
- Saying the landlord forfeits before count_days shows the 30 days passed, or when a proper notice came.
- Stopping at the forfeiture without saying the landlord may still sue for damages.
- Leaving out 83.49(5) when the tenant left early or had a periodic tenancy.
- Promising court costs or fees without the condition in 83.49(3)(c).

Yes, you can end your lease early. Under your lease, you have two primary contractual paths to do so (an early termination addendum or a lease transfer), as well as specific statutory grounds under Florida law if particular conditions apply.

Here is what each option costs and requires:

### 1. Early Termination (Addendum K)
Under Section 24.1 and Addendum K (Early Termination Addendum) of your lease, which implements Fla. Stat. § 83.595(4), you elected **Option 1: Liquidated Damages** (initialed "R.M.T.").

* **Fee:** An early termination fee of **$1,798.00** (which equals two months of your $899.00 installment).
* **Notice required:** You must give written notice at least **sixty (60) days** before your planned termination date. Notice must be delivered as required by Section 30.1: hand-delivered to the leasing office (requesting a date-stamped copy) or sent by certified mail with return receipt requested. Notice sent only by email, text, or the resident portal is not valid under Section 30.1.
* **Rent and other charges:** You must pay all rent installments and Additional Rent due through the termination date, as well as the $1,798.00 fee on or before that date (Addendum K; Fla. Stat. § 83.595(4)(a)).
* **Security deposit and damages:** The early termination fee does not cover physical damage to the bedroom or unit beyond normal wear and tear, which remains subject to deduction under Section 7 of the lease and Fla. Stat. § 83.49.

### 2. Lease Transfer to a Replacement (Addendum H)
Under Section 23.2 and Addendum H (Lease Transfer Addendum), you can transfer your lease to an approved replacement resident instead of paying the two months' termination fee. Note that direct subletting is prohibited (Section 23.1).

* **Transfer fee:** **$300.00** if you find the replacement yourself, or **$450.00** if Archer Commons finds the replacement from their transfer list (Addendum H, Section H-2.4).
* **Conditions:** The replacement resident must apply, meet rental standards, be approved, and sign a new lease; if the apartment is same-gender under roommate assignment policy, they must be acceptable to your roommates (Addendum H, Section H-2.2 and H-2.3).
* **Your liability:** All amounts owed through the transfer date must be paid. You remain responsible for rent and charges until the replacement's lease begins and all keys and access cards are returned (Addendum H, Section H-2.5 and H-3).

### 3. Florida Statutory Grounds (No Fee)
You may end the lease without paying an early termination fee if specific statutory situations apply:
* **Active Military Service:** Under Fla. Stat. § 83.682 and Section 24.1 of the lease, servicemembers entering active duty, receiving permanent change of station orders, or deploying may end the lease early by giving at least 30 days' written notice with copy of orders.
* **Casualty Damage:** Under Fla. Stat. § 83.63 and Section 31.2 of the lease, if the unit is substantially damaged or destroyed by fire or other casualty not caused by you or your guests so that enjoyment is substantially impaired, you may vacate and end the lease.
* **Landlord Failure to Maintain:** Under Fla. Stat. § 83.56(1), if the landlord materially fails to maintain the premises as required by Fla. Stat. § 83.51(1) or the lease, and does not correct the condition within 7 days after receiving proper written notice, you may terminate the rental agreement.

Note that graduating, withdrawing from school, transferring, or studying abroad does not relieve you of the lease (Section 24.2).

### What It Costs Under the Lease
Under Paragraph 18 of your lease, ending the lease early requires:
* **Early termination fee:** $2,200.00 (equal to two months’ rent at $1,100.00 per month, Paragraph 3), which must be paid by the date you move out.
* **Notice:** At least 60 days’ advance written notice.
* **Rent during notice:** You remain responsible for regular monthly rent ($1,100.00 per month under Paragraph 3) through your move-out date. Under Fla. Stat. § 83.595(4)(a), the landlord is entitled to rent and charges accrued through the end of the month in which the landlord retakes possession.

If you give the 60 days' notice, pay the $2,200.00 fee by move-out, and return the keys, Paragraph 18 states you owe no rent for any period after you move out. Under Fla. Stat. § 83.595(4), a landlord may charge an early termination fee only if the tenant accepted the fee by signing a **separate addendum** to the rental agreement containing specific statutory language and check-boxes. 

The four pages of your lease contain Paragraph 18, but no separate addendum:

* **If you did sign a separate early termination addendum:** Paragraph 18 applies as written. Paying the $2,200.00 fee and giving 60 days' notice limits your future rent liability.
* **If no separate addendum was signed:** Under Fla. Stat. § 83.595(4), the landlord cannot legally enforce the $2,200.00 early termination fee. Instead, if you break the lease early, the landlord's remedies are governed by Fla. Stat. § 83.595(1)–(3):

  3. Stand by and hold you liable as rent comes due each month (Fla. Stat. § 83.595(3)).

Under the reletting option (Fla. Stat. § 83.595(2)), your cost would depend on how quickly a replacement tenant is found: it could cost less than $2,200.00 if relet quickly, or more if the duplex sits vacant.

No, you cannot pay a fee to end your lease early under your current lease. 

In section 16 of your lease ("EARLY TERMINATION"), the box is checked for: 
"[X] This lease does not include an early termination option. If Tenant moves out early, Tenant is responsible for rent as Florida law provides." 
The option to pay an early termination fee was left unchecked.

Under Fla. Stat. § 83.595(4), an early termination fee is only available if both you and the landlord agreed to it at the time the lease was signed. Because that option was not selected, you do not have a contractual right to pay a set fee to end the lease.

If you move out early without a separate agreement, Fla. Stat. § 83.595 allows your landlord to choose among these remedies:
1. Treat the lease as terminated and retake possession, ending your liability for future rent (Fla. Stat. § 83.595(1));
2. Retake possession for your account and try in good faith to re-rent the apartment, holding you responsible for the difference between your rent and what is recovered (Fla. Stat. § 83.595(2)); or
3. Do nothing and hold you responsible for the rent as it comes due each month (Fla. Stat. § 83.595(3)).

You can still contact your landlord to ask whether they are willing to negotiate a mutual early termination agreement, but they are not legally required to agree to one.

The landlord must provide such written notice to the tenant in a manner prescribed by s. 83.56 (4) within 15 days before the start of the notification period contained in the rental agreement. The written notice must list all fees, penalties, and other charges applicable to the tenant under this subsection.
